sections.h2: Who runs the property tax office in Wilmington?
sections.html:
Valuing real estate, mailing bills and taking payments all happen at the county Tax Department, 230 Government Center Drive, Wilmington. Its phone line is (910) 798-7300, and the reappraisal team answers by email at reappraisal@nhcgov.com.

The county explains that your bill comes from two ingredients: your property's assessed value and a rate per $100 that elected county and municipal boards adopt. Those boards usually settle the rate in June. The county sets assessed value at 100% of estimated market value, as determined in the latest revaluation.

sections.h2: What are the 2026-27 rates in the county and its towns?
sections.html:
The county's general rate was set at 30.6 cents per $100 for the 2026-2027 fiscal year. Location adds more: Wilmington and three beach towns levy rates of their own on top of the county's.

sections.h2: How and when do owners pay the bill?
sections.html:
Bills are mailed ahead of a September 1 due date, and the county accepts payment without interest through January 5. After that, interest begins under G.S. 105-360.

Each bill carries four coupons, one for each quarter of the total, so a household can pay in pieces. The county lists these ways to pay:

  • Debit or credit card, or an e-check, at the Tax Office counter.
  • InvoiceCloud online, which carries a service fee, or 1-877-309-0878 by phone.
  • A drop box outside, just right of the Government Center entrance.
  • A mailed check, addressed to PO Box 18000, Wilmington, NC 28406.

Owners whose lender pays from escrow receive a courtesy notice, and they should check that the lender actually paid. If January 5 might slip by, phone the office before January 6 and ask about a payment plan.

sections.h2: How often does the county redo home values?
sections.html:
Every four years. The state minimum is eight, yet the commissioners chose four in 2008 because the county was growing so quickly, and the first four-year round started January 1, 2012. Today's values are as of January 1, 2025, with the following revaluation set for January 1, 2029.

For analysis the county sorts roughly 115,000 parcels into about 1,500 neighborhoods. Appraisers study home and land sales, make field and desk reviews, and use aerial imagery and computer models, then publish a Schedule of Values that the commissioners must approve. Outside a revaluation, a parcel's value shifts for reasons such as new building, damage, corrected records or a new use, while ordinary market swings wait until the next round.

A house still being built on January 1 is taxed at whatever stage it has reached, then at full value the following year. Owners do not re-list real property each year, yet any new improvements must be reported in January, and Tax Department staff will do the listing for those who ask.

sections.h2: How does the county define the value on your notice?
sections.html:
The county treats assessed value as fair market value, the likeliest price at which an informed buyer and seller, neither one rushed, would trade the property. Purchase cost, insurance value and rebuilding cost do not count as assessed value.

In a revaluation year, local boards publish a revenue-neutral rate, one that would raise the same money as the year before, and they are free to adopt a higher or lower figure. A jump in value therefore does not guarantee a bigger bill, because the rate can move too. Compare both numbers before you decide to appeal.

sections.h2: How can an owner contest a value in this county?
sections.html:
Use the county's appeal form, which costs nothing and needs no lawyer. Appeals open the day the value notice arrives and close when the board adjourns. For tax year 2026 the cutoff was 5:00 pm on May 14, 2026, so that window has shut. Filing within 30 days of the notice is encouraged, which gives staff time to look at the file before any hearing.

Proof is the owner's job. The county suggests bringing:

  • Sales of comparable homes that closed before January 1, 2025.
  • Photos showing condition or defects.
  • Notes on improvements the record gets wrong.
  • A formal appraisal dated before January 1, 2025, which is optional.

A dispute that survives informal review goes to the Board of Equalization and Review, which the county describes as local residents drawn from brokerage, appraisal, construction and law, sitting in smaller panels. Owners may appear or send papers instead. The board meets in the April to early May window, and its written ruling follows within 30 days. A further appeal goes to the state Property Tax Commission.

Any joint owner can file for the group. A business owner may send an officer, manager, W-2 employee or 25% owner. Other non-attorney helpers are limited to hardship cases such as illness, a death in the family or military deployment. Commercial owners are asked for three years of income and expense statements and a rent roll dated before January 1, 2025.

sections.h2: Can a senior, veteran or disabled owner in Wilmington cut the bill?
sections.html:
Three state programs exist for older, disabled and veteran owners, and the county's FAQ names each one. An owner gets only one, and the application is Form AV-9, which goes to the assessor.

  • Elderly or disabled exclusion: the greater of $25,000 or half of appraised value is set aside, with a 2026 income ceiling of $38,800.
  • Disabled veteran exclusion: $45,000 of value is set aside, and NCDOR's form says no age or income limit applies.
  • Circuit breaker: the bill is capped at 4.0% of income, or at 5.0% where income lies between the ceiling and $58,200. Five years of owning and living in the home are required.

File in January if you can, though forms are accepted through June 1 before the tax year. Circuit breaker enrollees reapply yearly, and taxes above the cap are put off rather than waived, so a sale brings back the preceding three years.

sections.h2: What happens to back taxes if you sell a house here?
sections.html:
Unpaid property tax is a lien on the parcel under G.S. 105-355, and a sale does not erase it. Call the Tax Department on (910) 798-7300 for what is owed, and give that figure to your closing attorney.

If nothing is paid, the county can foreclose through the courts under G.S. 105-374. Paying the balance from sale proceeds closes off that path.

sections.h2: What does the Census Bureau say about the county's housing market?
sections.html:
QuickFacts puts the 2025 population at 245,959, a 9.0% gain on April 2020, across 192.26 land square miles. In 2020 that worked out to 1,174.0 residents per square mile. A median owner-occupied house was worth $387,800 in the 2020 to 2024 data, and monthly owner costs were $1,888 with a mortgage and $658 without.

The median household took in $75,166. Another figure: 21.3% of residents are 65 or older, the age group the exclusions above were written for. Permits numbered 2,332 in 2025, so many owners have new work to list.

faqs.q: Which day do New Hanover County property tax bills come due?
faqs.a: They are due September 1, and the county takes payment without interest until January 5. Interest starts on January 6.

faqs.q: What is the county rate this fiscal year?
faqs.a: The county levies 30.6 cents per $100 in fiscal year 2026-2027, and unincorporated owners add 7.25 cents for fire services. Wilmington and the beach towns add municipal rates.

faqs.q: What year are values reset next?
faqs.a: The county schedules it for January 1, 2029. Values now in effect date from January 1, 2025.

faqs.q: Does it cost money to appeal a value?
faqs.a: There is no fee, and you do not need an attorney. For the current values, sales and appraisals offered as evidence should predate January 1, 2025.

faqs.q: Who pays the county for taxes still owed at a sale?
faqs.a: The lien stays on the parcel until paid. Request the payoff figure from the Tax Department so the closing attorney can pay it from proceeds.
